### 1.2 Our Techniques

In this section, we highlight our main techniques used in the algorithms and lower bounds.

#### Detection algorithms.

The previous algorithms for $k$ -clique detection in $n$ -node graphs [nesetril1985complexity, eisenbrand2004complexity] can be viewed as reductions to triangle detection, as mentioned earlier. Here is how they work when $k$ is not necessarily divisible by $3$ . For some integers $a,b,c\in[1,k]$ where $a+b+c=k$ , the algorithm creates a tripartite graph on node parts $A,B,C$ with $n^{a},n^{b},n^{c}$ nodes respectively, which represent tuples of $a,b,c$ nodes respectively. It also suffices to keep only the tuples of nodes that form a clique in the original graph. For every node $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{a})\in A$ and every node $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{b})\in B$ , the algorithm adds an edge between them if and only if $u_{1},\ldots,u_{a},v_{1},\ldots,v_{b}$ form an $(a+b)$ -clique in the original graph. It similarly adds edges between $B,C$ and between $A,C$ . It is not difficult to see that there is a triangle in the new graph if and only if there is a $k$ -clique in the original graph, so we can simply detect triangles by multiplying an $|A|\times|B|$ matrix with a $|B|\times|C|$ matrix.

We generalize this approach to $k$ -clique detection in terms of the number of $\ell$ -cliques for $\ell<k$ .

Suppose we are given a list of all $\ell$ -cliques in the graph, and we want to find a $k$ -clique. Let $a,b,c\in[1,k]$ be as before where $a+b+c=k$ . Let $A$ , $B$ , and $C$ , respectively, be the sets of $a$ -, $b$ - and $c$ -cliques in the graph. We would like to bound their sizes in terms of $\Delta_{\ell}$ . Let us focus on bounding $|A|$ ; bounding $|B|,|C|$ is done similarly.

For $a\geq\ell$ , a (probably folklore) bound shows that $\Delta_{a}\leq O(\Delta_{\ell}^{a/\ell})$ (we also provide a proof for completeness in Section 2).

For $a<\ell$ , we set a parameter $\Lambda$ and consider two types of $a$ -cliques: “low-degree” ones that are contained in $<\Lambda$ $\ell$ -cliques, and “high-degree” ones that are contained in $\geq\Lambda$ $\ell$ -cliques. There are at most $O(\Delta_{\ell}/\Lambda)$ high-degree $a$ -cliques.

Consider a low-degree $a$ -clique $K$ and its neighborhood consisting of the nodes adjacent to all nodes of $K$ . We can recurse on the neighborhood: find a $(k-a)$ -clique, given the list of $(\ell-a)$ -cliques formed by excluding $K$ from all $\ell$ -cliques that contain $K$ . We can bound the recursion runtime using the fact that $K$ has low degree. Since we have handled all low-degree $a$ -cliques, we can set $A$ to be only the $O(\Delta_{\ell}/\Lambda)$ high-degree $a$ -cliques. Similarly, we can get bounds on $|B|$ and $|C|$ .

Finally, following previous $k$ -clique detection algorithms [nesetril1985complexity, eisenbrand2004complexity], we perform a rectangular matrix multiplication between an $|A|\times|B|$ matrix and a $|B|\times|C|$ matrix. By analyzing the recursive steps and setting parameters appropriately, we obtain our detection runtimes. As we show in Examples 3.3 and 3.4, our recursion and its analysis are more careful than in prior work, allowing us to obtain improved runtimes for $4$ and $5$ -clique detection.

We give some explicit examples of this algorithm in Section 3.2. We also analyze the asymptotic efficiency of this algorithm in Section 3.3 and Section 3.4.

#### Lower bounds for listing.

We obtain our lower bound in Theorem 1.10 for listing from the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis. Our lower bound technique can be seen as a generalization of the reduction from Exact Triangle to triangle listing problems in [williams2020monochromatic].

We note that there is also a different generalization of the technique of [williams2020monochromatic] that shows a conditional lower bound for the $k$ -Set-Intersection problem [BringmannCM22]. We briefly describe the problem. At a very high level, the lower bound of [BringmannCM22] applies to the following hypergraph problem: the nodes are partitioned into $k+1$ parts: $V_{1},\ldots,V_{k}$ (these correspond to the sets) and $U$ (this corresponds to the universe). There are hyperedges among the nodes in $V_{1},\ldots,V_{k}$ (corresponding to $k$ -set-intersection queries) and there are edges between $U$ and $V_{i}$ for $i\in[k]$ (corresponding to elements belonging to each set). Given this hypergraph, the problem asks for each hyperedge, whether its nodes share a common neighbor in $U$ (i.e., whether the sets intersect). As the lower bound of [BringmannCM22] is for a problem in a hypergraph with hyperedges of cardinality $>2$ , it does not directly apply to our applications. Hypergraph problems are generally harder than their graph counterparts (see e.g. [LincolnWW18]), and there is no easy way to convert a hardness proof for hypergraphs into one for graphs without increasing the instance size significantly.

Now, we describe the high-level ideas of our reduction. Without loss of generality, we can assume the input instance of Exact- $k$ -Clique is a $k$ -partite graph on nodes $V_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_{k}$ , where each $V_{i}$ contains $n$ nodes. At a high level, we first hash the edge weights so that they behave random enough. For simplicity, we assume all edge weights are independently uniformly at random from $[-n^{k},n^{k}]$ in this overview (we deal with the randomness properly in our proof). Then we split $[-n^{k},n^{k}]$ equally into $s$ contiguous intervals, each of size $O(n^{k}/s)$ for some parameter $s$ . We then enumerate combinations of intervals $(L_{i,j})_{1\leq i<j\leq k}$ , and consider the subgraph where we only keep edges between $V_{i}$ and $V_{j}$ whose weight is in $L_{i,j}$ . Note that a subgraph cannot contain a $k$ -clique of weight $0$ if $0\not\in\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}L_{i,j}$ (we denote the sum of two intervals as the sumset of them). Therefore, we only need to consider combinations of intervals where $0\in\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}L_{i,j}$ . If we choose the first $\binom{k}{2}-1$ intervals $(L_{i,j})_{1\leq i<j\leq k,(i,j)\neq(k-1,k)}$ , the final interval must intersect $-\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k,(i,j)\neq(k-1,k)}L_{i,j}$ , which has size $O(\frac{n^{k}}{s})$ . Therefore, there are only $O(1)$ choices for the final interval, and the total number of combinations of intervals we need to consider is $O(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1})$ .

For each combination of intervals, we form the subgraph only containing edges with weights in the intervals, and we list all the $k$ -cliques in this subgraph. The expected number of $\ell$ -cliques in the subgraph is $O(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}})$ and the expected number of $k$ -cliques is $O(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}})$ . For simplicity, we assume these upper bounds always hold in this overview (instead of only holding in expectation). Also, we can list all the $\ell$ -cliques in the subgraphs efficiently, i.e., in nearly linear time in their number, which is faster than $n^{k}$ when $s$ is small enough.

Then suppose we have an $O\left(\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-\varepsilon}\right)$ time algorithm for listing all $k$ -cliques in a graph with $t$ $k$ -cliques and with a given list of $\Delta_{\ell}$ $\ell$ -cliques. We can list all $k$ -cliques in all the subgraphs in time

$$ \tilde{O}\left(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\left(\left(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}\left(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}\right)^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-\varepsilon}\right)=\tilde{O}\left(n^{k-k\varepsilon}\left(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\right)^{\varepsilon}\right), $$

which is $\tilde{O}(n^{k-\varepsilon^{\prime}})$ time for $\varepsilon^{\prime}>0$ for sufficiently small $s$ , and violates the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis.

#### Listing algorithms for graphs with a large number $t$ of $k$ -cliques.

Here we discuss how we obtain our optimal algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ in Theorem 1.11, for all $\ell<k$ and large enough $t$ . We give the full algorithm in Section 5. The framework works for all values of $t$ , but the runtime is conditionally optimal only for large $t$ . We will later explain how to improve upon the framework for small $t$ .

As a first step, we obtain output-sensitive algorithms for $k$ -clique listing in terms of $n$ ( $\ell=1$ ). We then use these algorithms in a black-box way for $\ell\geq 2$ .

Björklund, Pagh, Vassilevska W. and Zwick [bjorklund2014listing] gave an algorithm for triangle listing using a dense-sparse paradigm. We generalize this algorithm to $k\geq 4$ . Let $t$ be the number of $k$ -cliques in the graph which we want to list.

- • Dense algorithm: When the input graph has many edges, we use sampling and rectangular matrix multiplication to find all the edges that occur in at most $\lambda$ $k$ -cliques, for some parameter $\lambda$ . We then list all $k$ -cliques incident to such edges, and can then delete these edges to obtain a graph with at most $O(t/\lambda)$ edges. We then call the algorithm for sparse graphs.

- • Sparse algorithm: When the input graph has few edges, we list all $k$ -cliques incident to nodes with degree at most $x$ by listing $(k-1)$ -cliques in their neighborhoods, for some parameter $x$ . We are then left with a graph with at most $O(m/x)$ nodes, at which point we call the dense algorithm.

The key change from the framework of [bjorklund2014listing] is in the sparse algorithm. There, [bjorklund2014listing] uses brute-force to list triangles through low-degree nodes. We on the other hand, recursively use $(k-1,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithms to list the $(k-1)$ -cliques in the neighborhoods of low-degree nodes. This makes our algorithm efficient, but also complicates the analysis significantly.

For $\ell\geq 2$ , we exploit recursion even more: we recursively use algorithms for both $k$ -clique listing in terms of nodes, and $(k-1)$ -clique listing in terms of $(\ell-1)$ -cliques. At a high level, we first find all nodes that are contained in at most $y$ $\ell$ -cliques, for some parameter $y$ . Then, in the neighborhoods of such nodes, we can find all $(k-1)$ -cliques based on the list of all $(\ell-1)$ -cliques in the neighborhood. We can then delete all the low-degree nodes. The resulting graph now only has $O(\Delta_{\ell}/y)$ nodes. Now, we can call the $k$ -clique listing algorithm in terms of $n$ .

Because of the extra recursion, the analysis gets more complicated, but we are able to keep the algorithms relatively simple. Thus we get the best of both worlds: simplicity and optimality (at least for large $t$ ).

The reason why our $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm is only optimal for large $t$ is that our dense algorithm has an inherent cost of $\Omega(n^{k-1})$ due to the rectangular matrix multiplication that we use. This bottleneck extends to $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for all $\ell$ as well since all of these algorithms call $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ .

#### Generalizing the listing algorithm to all values of $t$ .

In Section 6, we explain how to improve upon our listing framework above when $t$ is smaller. While our general runtime analysis for arbitrary $k,t$ and $\ell$ quickly gets complicated, here we will focus on a small example, to give intuition.

Let us consider the example of $6$ -clique listing in an $n$ -node graph $G$ assuming $\omega=2$ . The algorithm in Theorem 1.11 has runtime $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{2}{5}}t^{\frac{14}{15}})$ only when $t\geq n^{4+\frac{13}{14}}$ , and otherwise runs in $\tilde{O}(n^{5})$ time33 3 Clearly, when $t$ is smaller, the runtime can only be smaller or equal, so for any $t<n^{4+\frac{13}{14}}$ , the runtime of this algorithm is $\tilde{O}(n^{\frac{2}{5}}(n^{4+\frac{13}{14}})^{\frac{14}{15}})=\tilde{O}(n^{5})$ when $\omega=2$ . which is worse than the $6$ -clique detection runtime $\tilde{O}(n^{4})$ .

We improve the runtime for $t$ smaller than the threshold of $n^{4+\frac{13}{14}}$ by instead following the techniques of [nesetril1985complexity, eisenbrand2004complexity]. We create a new graph $G^{\prime}$ whose nodes correspond to the pairs of nodes of the original graph $G$ , i.e. the new graph has $n^{2}$ nodes. We then add an edge between two nodes $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ if $(a,b,c,d)$ forms a $4$ -clique in the original graph. Now, we run the triangle listing algorithm (in [bjorklund2014listing] or Theorem 1.11) in the new graph. This has runtime $\tilde{O}(n^{2}t^{2/3})$ when $t\geq(n^{2})^{1.5}=n^{3}$ . This also allows us to obtain an algorithm for all $t\leq n^{3}$ , running in time $\tilde{O}(n^{4})$ , the $6$ -clique detection runtime, which is tight under Hypothesis 1.1.

The corresponding runtime is depicted in blue in Figure 3.

More generally, for larger $k$ , we create a new graph where the nodes represent $\ell^{\prime}$ -cliques in the original graph. Then, we list $\lceil k/\ell^{\prime}\rceil$ -cliques in the new graph. The best $\ell^{\prime}$ varies for different $t$ , and this gives us the trade-offs as seen in Figure 2.

Roughly speaking, the algorithm can be viewed as using different dimensions of rectangular matrix multiplication depending on the value of $t$ . For example, in the case of $k=6$ , the algorithm for large $t\geq n^{4+\frac{13}{14}}$ uses $\tilde{O}(\lambda)$ matrix multiplications of size roughly $n\times n^{4}/\lambda$ by $n^{4}/\lambda\times n$ for some parameter $\lambda\geq 1$ , and this requires at least $\Omega(n^{5})$ time. For $n^{3}\leq t\leq n^{4+\frac{13}{14}}$ , the algorithm uses $\tilde{O}(\rho)$ matrix multiplications of size $n^{2}\times n^{2}/\rho$ by $n^{2}/\rho\times n^{2}$ for some parameter $\rho\geq 1$ , which requires at least $\Omega(n^{4})$ time.

### 1.3 Organization

In Section 2, we give necessary definitions and standard algorithms. In Section 3, we show our framework for detecting cliques. In Section 4, we show our lower bound for listing cliques, proving Theorem 1.10. In Section 5, we show our optimal algorithm for clique listing in graphs with many $k$ -cliques, and we extend this algorithm to graphs with fewer $k$ -cliques in Section 6. Finally, we show a more efficient algorithm for $6$ -clique listing in Section 7.

## 2 Preliminaries

#### Notation.

Throughout this paper, we denote the number of nodes in a graph by $n$ , the number of edges by $m$ , and the number of $\ell$ -cliques by $\Delta_{\ell}$ . For an $\ell^{\prime}$ -clique $K$ for some $1\leq\ell^{\prime}\leq\ell$ , we use $\Delta_{\ell}(K)$ to denote the number of $\ell$ -cliques containing $K$ . For the special case of $\ell=2$ , we use $\deg(v):=\Delta_{2}(v)$ . For integer $k$ , we use $K_{k}$ to denote a $k$ -clique.

For a nonnegative integer $n$ , we use $[n]$ to denote $\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ .

#### Matrix multiplication.

We use $\omega<2.372$ to denote the matrix multiplication exponent [duan2023, VXXZ24]. For any constants $a,b,c\geq 0$ , we use $\omega(a,b,c)$ to denote the exponent of multiplying an $n^{a}\times n^{b}$ matrix by an $n^{b}\times n^{c}$ matrix. The current best bounds for rectangular matrix multiplication are given by [VXXZ24].

We denote by $\mathsf{MM}(A,B,C)$ the runtime of multiplying an $A\times B$ by a $B\times C$ matrix. If $A\leq B\leq C$ , we can loosely bound $\mathsf{MM}(A,B,C)$ in terms of $\omega$ as follows:

$$ \mathsf{MM}(A,B,C)\leq O\left(A^{\omega}\cdot\frac{BC}{A^{2}}\right)=O(A^{\omega-2}BC). $$

This bound is obtained by splitting the matrix multiplication into $\frac{B}{A}\cdot\frac{C}{A}$ instances of square matrix multiplication of size $A$ , and it is in general weaker than the bound in [LU18].

#### Hölder’s Inequality.

To analyze the runtime of our algorithms, we often utilize a reformulation of Hölder’s inequality.

#### Lemma 2.1 (Hölder’s Inequality).

Given $p,q\in(1,\infty)$ such that $1/p+1/q=1$ , the following inequality holds for any $x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\geq 0$ :

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}y_{k}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{p}\right)^{1/p}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{k}^{q}\right)^{1/q}. $$

We restate Hölder’s Inequality as follows. This is the version that we use in our runtime analyses.

#### Corollary 2.2.

Given $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$ such that $\alpha+\beta=1$ , the following inequality holds for any $x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\geq 0$ :

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}^{\alpha}y_{k}^{\beta}\leq\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{k}\right)^{\alpha}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}y_{k}\right)^{\beta} $$

### 2.1 Problem Definitions

Now, we define the main clique problems that we consider in this paper.

#### Definition 2.3 ( $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ ).

Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and the list $L$ of all $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ , decide whether $G$ contains a $k$ -clique.

#### Definition 2.4 ( $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ ).

Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ and the list $L$ of all $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ , list all $k$ -cliques in $G$ .

In $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ , we use $t$ to denote the total number of $k$ -cliques in the graph. However, as we will show in Section 2.2, we can equivalently (up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factor) use $t$ to denote the number of $k$ -cliques we wish to list.

### 2.2 Basic Clique Listing Algorithms

Next, we give some standard algorithms and reductions.

#### Lemma 2.5.

Suppose $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ can be solved in time $D(\Delta_{\ell})$ . Then, given the list of all $\ell$ -cliques in a graph, one can find a $k$ -clique in $\tilde{O}(D(\Delta_{\ell}))$ time.

#### Proof.

Let the input graph be $G=(V,E)$ , with list $L$ of all $\ell$ -cliques. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $|V|\leq O(\Delta_{\ell})$ by deleting all nodes that are not in any $\ell$ -clique (since such a node cannot be in a $k$ -clique).

If $|V|\leq k$ , brute force and check if the graph has a $k$ -clique. Otherwise, run $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ on the graph. If it has a $k$ -clique, arbitrarily partition $V$ into $k+1$ sets, $V_{1},\dots,V_{k+1}$ . Now, for each $i\in[k+1],$ consider the subgraph on node set $V_{-i}=\cup_{j\in[k+1]\setminus\{i\}}V_{j}$ , and run $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . Note that each such subgraph contains at most $\Delta_{\ell}$ $\ell$ -cliques. For some $i$ , it must be the case that the graph on $V_{-i}$ contains a $k$ -clique as we partitioned into $k+1$ parts and a $k$ -clique has only $k$ nodes. Recurse on exactly one such subgraph $V_{-i}$ on which the detection algorithm returned “YES”.

Since the depth of this recursion is $O(\log_{\frac{k+1}{k}}|V|)=O(\log\Delta_{\ell})$ , and we call $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ on $O(1)$ instances at each step, we have a runtime of $\tilde{O}(D(\Delta_{\ell}))$ as desired. ∎

#### Lemma 2.6.

$(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in time $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{k/\ell})$ .

#### Proof.

We will prove by induction on the following stronger statement: given a list $L$ of $\ell$ -cliques in a graph (not necessarily all $\ell$ -cliques), one can list all $k$ -cliques covered by these $\ell$ -cliques in the graph in time $\tilde{O}\left(|L|^{k/\ell}\right)$ , where a $k$ -clique $K$ is covered by a list $L$ of $\ell$ -cliques if every $\ell$ -clique subgraph of $K$ lies in $L$ .

When $\ell=1$ , it suffices to use brute-force to list all $k$ -cliques. Now suppose $\ell>1$ .

First, we find all $(\ell-1)$ -cliques that are contained in at most $x$ (and at least $1$ ) $\ell$ -cliques in the list in $O(|L|)$ time. If an $(\ell-1)$ -clique $K$ is contained in $y\leq x$ $\ell$ -cliques in the list, then we can list all $k$ -cliques containing $K$ in $\tilde{O}(y^{k-\ell+1})\leq\tilde{O}(y\cdot x^{k-\ell})$ time by brute-force. Over all such $(\ell-1)$ -cliques, the total running time is thus $\tilde{O}(|L|x^{k-\ell})$ .

The number of $(\ell-1)$ -cliques that are contained in at least one of the $\ell$ -cliques in $L$ and are not considered above is $O(|L|/x)$ . Let $L^{\prime}$ be the list of these $O(|L|/x)$ $(\ell-1)$ -cliques. If a $k$ -clique $K$ is not found above, then all of its $(\ell-1)$ -clique subgraphs are in the list $L^{\prime}$ , i.e., $K$ is covered by $L^{\prime}$ . By induction, we can find the list of all $k$ -cliques that are covered by $(\ell-1)$ -cliques in $L^{\prime}$ in $\tilde{O}((|L|/x)^{k/(\ell-1)})$ time. This combined with the $k$ -cliques listed in the previous case gives all the $k$ -cliques covered by $L$ .

Setting $x=|L|^{1/\ell}$ gives the desired $\tilde{O}(|L|^{k/\ell})$ time, and thus completes the induction. ∎

The proof of Lemma 2.6 also implies that the number of $k$ -cliques in a graph with $\Delta_{\ell}$ $\ell$ -cliques is $O(\Delta_{\ell}^{k/\ell})$ .

#### Lemma 2.7.

Fix $1\leq\ell<k$ . Suppose there is a $T(\Delta_{\ell},x)$ time algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ where the total number of $k$ -cliques is $\Theta(\Delta_{\ell}^{x})$ . Then for any $x^{\prime}<x$ , $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ on graphs where the total number of $k$ -cliques is $\Theta(\Delta_{\ell}^{x^{\prime}})$ can be solved in $O(T(\Delta_{\ell},x))$ time.

#### Proof.

First of all, by Lemma 2.6, $x\leq\frac{k}{\ell}$ . We then add a complete $k$ -partite graph to the graph where the number of nodes in each part is $\Delta_{\ell}^{x/k}$ . This way, the number of $k$ -cliques in the graph is increased by $\Delta_{\ell}^{x}$ , and the number of $\ell$ -cliques is increased by $\Delta_{\ell}^{\ell x/k}\leq\Delta_{\ell}$ . Thus, the number of $k$ -cliques in the graph is $(\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell})^{x}$ , where $\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell}=\Theta(\Delta_{\ell})$ is the new number of $\ell$ -cliques in the graph. Therefore, we can run the $T(\Delta_{\ell},x)$ time algorithm on the new graph in $\Theta(T(\Delta_{\ell},x))$ time. Once we list all the $k$ -cliques in the new graph, we can return those that belong to the original graph. ∎

Let $f(\Delta_{\ell},t)$ be the runtime of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ when the graph has (an unknown number of) $t$ cliques in total, and let $g(\Delta_{\ell},t)$ be the runtime of listing $\min\{\Delta_{k},t\}$ distinct $k$ -cliques, given the list of all $\ell$ -cliques in the graph and a specified $t$ as input. We assume $f(\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}),\tilde{O}(t))=\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ and $g(\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}),\tilde{O}(t))=\tilde{O}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ . This is true for all of our algorithms as well as any algorithm that has at most a polynomial dependence on $\Delta_{\ell}$ and $t$ .

The following lemma shows that $f(\Delta_{\ell},t)=\tilde{\Theta}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ . Therefore, we use both of these two notions interchangeably for the definition of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ . In particular, given an instance of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ with an unknown number of $k$ -cliques, the proof of Lemma 2.8 allows us to assume that we know an $2$ -approximation of $\Delta_{k}$ , with only $\tilde{O}(1)$ loss in the running time.

#### Lemma 2.8.

$f(\Delta_{\ell},t)=\tilde{\Theta}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ .

#### Proof.

We first show $f(\Delta_{\ell},t)=\tilde{O}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ . Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm for listing a specified number of $k$ -cliques. Given an $n$ -node graph $G$ and the list of $\Delta_{\ell}$ cliques, we run $O(\log n)$ instances of $\mathcal{A}$ in parallel. More specifically, we specify these instances to list $2^{0},2^{1},\ldots,2^{\lceil\log(n^{k}+1)\rceil}$ $k$ -cliques respectively. We wait until one of the instances finishes listing all $k$ -cliques in the graph. Suppose $t$ is the actual number of $k$ -cliques in the graph, and we specify $\mathcal{A}$ to list $2^{\lceil\log t\rceil}$ $k$ -cliques, then it will finish within $g(\Delta_{\ell},O(t))=\tilde{O}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ time. Since we run $O(\log n)$ instances in parallel, the overall running time is $\tilde{O}(g(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ .

Next, we show $g(\Delta_{\ell},t)=\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ . Let $\mathcal{B}$ be an algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ . Given a graph $G=(V,E)$ , a list of all $\ell$ -cliques and a parameter $t$ , we need to list $\min\{t,\Delta_{k}\}$ $k$ -cliques in $\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ time. First, we run $\mathcal{B}$ for $\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},2^{k}t))=\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ time. By Lemma 2.7, if $\Delta_{k}\leq 2^{k}t$ , $\mathcal{B}$ will finish in $\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},2^{k}t)$ ) time, and we are done. Now, we assume the number of $k$ -cliques in $G$ is at least $2^{k}t$ .

We create a $k$ -partite graph $G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime})$ as follows. Let $V^{\prime}=V_{1}\sqcup\dots\sqcup V_{k}$ where each $V_{i}$ is a copy of $V$ . Let $v_{i}$ be the copy of node $v\in V$ in $V_{i}$ . Add edges $(u_{i},v_{j})$ between nodes $u_{i}\in V_{i}$ and $v_{j}\in V_{j}$ if and only if $i\neq j$ and $(u,v)\in E$ . Clearly, the number of $k$ -cliques in $G^{\prime}$ is at least $2^{k}(k!)t$ , and we need to list $(k!)t$ distinct $k$ -cliques in $G^{\prime}$ in order to produce $t$ distinct $k$ -cliques in $G$ . Also, the number of $\ell$ -cliques in $G^{\prime}$ is $O(\Delta_{\ell})$ . Then we partition each $V_{i}$ arbitrarily into two sets $V_{i,0}$ and $V_{i,1}$ of size $n/2$ . We run $\mathcal{B}$ on each of the $2^{k}$ induced subgraphs on the sets $V_{1,b_{1}},V_{2,b_{2}},\dots,V_{k,b_{k}}$ , where $b_{i}\in\{0,1\}$ for $\tilde{O}(f(O(\Delta_{\ell}),2^{k}(k!)t))=\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ time. By the pigenhole principle, one of the subgraphs contain at least $(k!)t$ $k$ -cliques. If $\mathcal{B}$ finishes on that subgraph, we are done. Otherwise, $\mathcal{B}$ does not finish on that subgraph, and by Lemma 2.7, that subgraph must have more than $2^{k}(k!)t$ distinct $k$ -cliques, so we can recurse on that induced subgraph. Overall, the running time is $\tilde{O}(f(\Delta_{\ell},t))$ because the recursion depth is $O(\log n)$ . ∎

[bjorklund2014listing] gave similar reductions from listing a specified number of $t$ triangles to listing all $\Delta_{3}$ triangles in $n$ -node or $m$ -edge graphs. Their reduction is more efficient than ours when $t$ is much smaller than $\Delta_{3}$ . However, their reduction requires an algorithm for counting the number of triangles. We instead provide a black box reduction that does not rely on counting, that works for arbitrary $k,\ell$ , and is more self-contained and efficient enough for our purpose.

## 3 Detecting Cliques

In this section, we first describe our algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ , and then analyze its running time in some interesting cases.

Throughout this section, we use $g(k,\ell)$ to denote our algorithm’s running time exponent on the number of $\ell$ -cliques of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ , i.e., our algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ runs in $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{g(k,\ell)})$ time.

### 3.1 General Detection Framework

Now we describe a generic algorithm for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ for $k\geq 3$ (for $k=2$ , we trivially list all edges in the graph, so $g(2,1)=2$ ) in Algorithm 1.

*Algorithm 1 Generic $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm.*

```
Input: Graph $G=(V,E)$ and the list $L$ of all $\ell$ -cliques.
Output: Output yes if $G$ contains a $k$ -cliques, and no otherwise.
The Algorithm: • Let integers $k\geq a\geq b\geq c\geq 1$ be such that $k=a+b+c$ (the algorithm chooses $a,b,c$ optimally). Then goal is then to bound the number of $d$ -cliques for $d\in\{a,b,c\}$ . – If $d\geq\ell$ , we can use Lemma 2.6 to upper bound the number of $d$ -cliques with $S_{d}=\tilde{\Theta}(\Delta_{\ell}^{d/\ell})$ , and add these $d$ -cliques to a list $L_{d}$ in the same time. – If $d<\ell$ , for every $d$ -clique $K$ with $\Delta_{\ell}(K)\leq\Delta_{\ell}^{x_{d}}$ (for some parameter $x_{d}\in[0,1]$ to be chosen), we check if $K$ is in a $k$ -clique by recursively running $(k-d,\ell-d)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ in its neighbourhood. Then, let $L_{d}$ denote the set of remaining $d$ -cliques. Then, $S_{d}:=|L_{d}|=\Theta(\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{d}})$ . The running time of this step is $\displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}K:d\text{-clique}\\ \Delta_{\ell}(K)\leq\Delta_{\ell}^{x_{d}}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{\ell}(K)^{g(k-d,\ell-d)}\right)$ $\displaystyle\leq\tilde{O}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}K:d\text{-clique}\\ \Delta_{\ell}(K)\leq\Delta_{\ell}^{x_{d}}\end{subarray}}\Delta_{\ell}(K)\cdot\Delta_{\ell}^{x_{d}(g(k-d,\ell-d)-1)}\right)$ $\displaystyle\leq\tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{d}(g(k-d,\ell-d)-1)}\right).$ • Finally, we conduct a usual matrix multiplication of dimensions $S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}$ in time $\mathsf{MM}(S_{a},S_{b},S_{c})$ as follows. If we find a $k$ -clique, output yes, otherwise we output no. – Create a matrix $X$ whose rows are indexed by $a$ -cliques in $L_{a}$ and columns are indexed by $b$ -cliques in $L_{b}$ . Set $A[K_{a},K_{b}]=1$ if the nodes of $K_{a}$ and $K_{b}$ form an $(a+b)$ -clique, and $0$ otherwise. – Create a matrix $Y$ whose rows are indexed by $b$ -cliques in $L_{b}$ and columns are indexed by $c$ -cliques in $L_{c}$ , and set the entries similarly. – Compute $Z=XY$ . For each pair of remaining $a$ -clique $K_{a}$ and $c$ -clique $K_{c}$ that form an $(a+c)$ -clique, check if $Z[K_{a},K_{c}]>0$ . If such an entry exists, output yes. Otherwise, output no.
```

The correctness of this algorithm is immediate. We also remark that the algorithm can be used to count the number of $k$ -cliques, by replacing all the recursive calls with the counting version of the algorithm, using the matrix multiplication to count the number of $k$ -cliques in the remaining graph, and properly summing up and scaling the numbers. Clearly, the counting version of the algorithm will have the same running time.

### 3.2 Examples

Let us give some explicit examples to illustrate the algorithm.

#### $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ .

The simplest example is $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ for $k\geq 3$ . Let $\lfloor k/3\rfloor\leq c\leq b\leq a\leq\lceil k/3\rceil$ be integers such that $a+b+c=k$ , which is one of the possible choices of $a,b,c$ for the algorithm. Note that $c=\lfloor k/3\rfloor,b=\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil,a=\lceil k/3\rceil$ . Since $a,b,c\geq\ell=1$ , the algorithm would choose to use Lemma 2.6 to bound the number of cliques of sizes $a,b,c$ as $n^{a},n^{b},n^{c}$ respectively. Thus, the running time of the algorithm is $\tilde{O}(n^{\omega(a,b,c)})=\tilde{O}(n^{\beta(k)})$ , matching the previous running time [eisenbrand2004complexity].

#### $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ for $\ell\leq\lfloor k/3\rfloor.$

Similar as above, let $c=\lfloor k/3\rfloor,b=\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil,a=\lceil k/3\rceil$ and the algorithm would choose to use Lemma 2.6 to bound the number of cliques of sizes $a,b,c$ . Thus, the running time of the algorithm is $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\omega(a/\ell,b/\ell,c/\ell)})\leq\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\omega(\lceil k/3\rceil,\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil,\lfloor k/3\rfloor)/\ell})$ . This running time is optimal barring improvements for $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ :

#### Proposition 3.1.

Fix any positive integers $k\geq 3$ and $\ell\leq\lfloor k/3\rfloor$ , and let $\beta(k)=\omega(\lceil k/3\rceil,\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil,\lfloor k/3\rfloor)$ . If $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ requires $n^{\beta(k)-o(1)}$ time, then $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ requires $\Delta_{\ell}^{\beta(k)/\ell-o(1)}$ time.

#### Proof.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ has an $O(\Delta_{\ell}^{\beta(k)/\ell-{\varepsilon}}$ ) time algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ for some ${\varepsilon}>0$ . Then given a $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ instance, we can first use Lemma 2.6 to list all $\ell$ -cliques in $O(n^{\ell})$ time, and the number of $\ell$ -cliques is bounded by $O(n^{\ell})$ . Then we can use $\mathcal{A}$ to solve the $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ instance in $O((n^{\ell})^{\beta(k)/\ell-{\varepsilon}})=n^{\beta(k)-{\varepsilon}\ell}$ time, a contradiction. ∎

#### Example 3.2 ( $(3,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ ).

In this case, the algorithm can only choose $a=b=c=1$ , and it would naturally choose $x_{a}=x_{b}=x_{c}$ . The time it takes to bound the number of $1$ -cliques (nodes) is $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{2}^{1+x_{a}(g(2,1)-1)})=\tilde{O}(m^{1+x_{a}})$ . Then we have $S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}\leq\Theta(m^{1-x_{a}})$ . Thus, the running time for the matrix multiplication of dimensions $S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}$ is $\tilde{O}(m^{(1-x_{a})\omega})$ . Overall, the running time is $\tilde{O}(m^{\frac{2\omega}{\omega+1}})$ by setting $x_{a}=\frac{\omega-1}{\omega+1}$ . This is essentially Alon, Yuster and Zwick [alon1997finding]’s triangle detection algorithm for sparse graphs.

#### Example 3.3 ( $(4,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ ).

In this case, the algorithm can only choose $a=2,b=c=1$ , and it would naturally choose $x_{b}=x_{c}$ . The algorithm uses Lemma 2.6 to (trivially) bound the number of edges as $m$ . The time it takes to bound the number of nodes is $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{2}^{1+x_{b}(g(3,1)-1)})=\tilde{O}(m^{1+x_{b}(\omega-1)})$ . Then we have $S_{a}\leq\Theta(m),S_{b},S_{c}\leq\Theta(m^{1-x_{b}})$ . Thus, the running time for the matrix multiplication of dimensions $S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}$ is $\tilde{O}(m^{\omega(1,1-x_{b},1-x_{b})})$ . The algorithm chooses $x_{b}$ so that $1+x_{b}(\omega-1)=\omega(1,1-x_{b},1-x_{b})$ . If we simply bound $\omega(1,1-x_{b},1-x_{b})$ by $x_{b}+\omega(1-x_{b})$ , we can get $g(4,2)\leq\frac{\omega+1}{2}$ by setting $x_{b}=\frac{1}{2}$ . For the current best bound of square and rectangular matrix multiplication [VXXZ24], we can set $x_{b}=0.478$ to get an upper bound $g(4,2)\leq 1.657$ . As seen in Table 2, this is an improvement over the previous best algorithm of Eisenbrand and Grandoni [eisenbrand2004complexity]. The key difference between our algorithm and [eisenbrand2004complexity]’s algorithm is that, after they perform a similar first stage, they recursively call a $(4,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm on graphs with $S_{b}$ nodes, losing the information that the graph has $S_{a}=m$ edges to begin with. We instead utilize this information with rectangular matrix multiplication to get a better running time.

#### Example 3.4 ( $(5,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ ).

In this case, let the algorithm choose $a=b=2,c=1$ (the choice $a=3,b=c=1$ gives a worse bound). The algorithm uses Lemma 2.6 to (trivially) bound the number of edges as $m$ . The time it takes to bound the number of nodes is $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{2}^{1+x_{c}(g(4,1)-1)})=\tilde{O}(m^{1+x_{c}(\omega(1,2,1)-1)})$ . Then we have $S_{a},S_{b}\leq\Theta(m),S_{c}\leq\Theta(m^{1-x_{c}})$ . Thus, the running time for the matrix multiplication of dimensions $S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}$ is $\tilde{O}(m^{\omega(1,1,1-x_{c})})$ . The algorithm chooses $x_{c}$ so that $1+x_{c}(\omega(1,2,1)-1)=\omega(1,1,1-x_{c})$ . If we simply bound $\omega(1,2,1)$ by $\omega+1$ and $\omega(1,1,1-x_{c})$ by $2x_{c}+(1-x_{c})\omega$ , we can get $g(5,2)\leq\frac{\omega+2}{2}$ by setting $x_{c}=\frac{1}{2}$ . For the current best bound of rectangular matrix multiplication [VXXZ24], we can set $x_{c}=0.469$ to get an upper bound $g(5,2)\leq 2.057$ . As seen in Table 2, this is an improvement over the previous best known algorithm of Eisenbrand and Grandoni [eisenbrand2004complexity].

#### Example 3.5 (More Small Examples).

See Tables 3 and 4 for more examples of the running times of our algorithm. These running times were obtained by finding the optimal values of $a,b,c$ using dynamic programming.

From previous examples, one might wonder whether the algorithm always sets $a,b,c$ as close to $k/3$ as possible. The following example shows that it is not the case (for $\omega=2$ ).

In $(8,4)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ , if the algorithm chooses $a=4,b=c=2$ , then the running time is

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{4}^{1+x_{b}(g(6,2)-1)}+\Delta_{4}^{1+x_{c}(g(6,2)-1)}+\Delta_{4}^{\omega(1,1-x_{b},1-x_{c})}\right). $$

By setting $x_{b}=x_{c}=\frac{1}{2}$ , this running time is bounded by $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{4}^{3/2})$ when $\omega=2$ (See Table 4 for the value of $g(6,2)$ when $\omega=2$ ).

However, if the algorithm chooses a more balanced choice $a=b=3,c=2$ , then the running time is

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{4}^{1+x_{a}(g(5,1)-1)}+\Delta_{4}^{1+x_{b}(g(5,1)-1)}+\Delta_{4}^{1+x_{c}(g(6,2)-1)}+\Delta_{4}^{\omega(1-x_{a},1-x_{b},1-x_{c})}\right). $$

One optimal way to set the parameters when $\omega=2$ is $x_{a}=x_{b}=\frac{1}{5}$ and $x_{c}=\frac{3}{5}$ , which only gives an $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{4}^{8/5})$ running time when $\omega=2$ (See Table 4 for the values of $g(5,1)$ and $g(6,2)$ when $\omega=2$ ).

### 3.3 Upper Bound for $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$

In this section, we analyze the running time of our algorithm for $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ for some constant $h=O(1)$ . For convenience, let $e_{h}(k)=g(k,k-h)$ .

We start with the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.6.

For every $k>h$ , $e_{h}(k+1)\leq e_{h}(k)$ .

#### Proof.

We prove the statement by induction. We skip the base case $k=h+1$ as it works similarly as the induction step (except for $h=1$ , in which case $e_{h}(2)=2$ and $e_{h}(3)=\frac{2\omega}{\omega+1}\leq e_{h}(2)$ , as the algorithm handles $(2,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ specially). Suppose the statement is already true for all smaller $k$ .

Let $\ell=k-h$ and $\ell^{\prime}=k+1-h$ . Suppose for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ , the optimal parameters are $a,b,c,x_{a},x_{b},x_{c},S_{a},S_{b},S_{c}$ ( $x_{d}$ is relevant only if $d<\ell$ for $d\in\{a,b,c\}$ ). Consider $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ with parameters $a^{\prime}=a+1,b^{\prime}=b,c^{\prime}=c$ and $x^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}},x^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}},x^{\prime}_{c^{\prime}},S^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}},S^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}},S^{\prime}_{c^{\prime}}$ to be determined. Let $\Delta_{\ell}$ be the number of $\ell$ -cliques in the $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ instance and let $\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}}$ be the number of $(\ell+1)$ -cliques in the $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ instance.

We first compare exponents related to $S_{a}$ and $S^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}$ .

- • If $a\geq\ell$ . Then $S_{a}$ in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ is bounded by $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{a/\ell})$ . In the $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm, $S_{a^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ is bounded by $\tilde{O}((\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{(a+1)/(\ell+1)})$ , a smaller exponent.

- • If $a<\ell$ , the exponent of the running time for bounding $S_{a}$ in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ is $1+x_{a}(e_{h}(k-a)-1)$ , and $S_{a}$ is bounded by $\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{a}}$ . Let $x^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}$ be equal to $x_{a}$ in the algorithm for $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . Then notice that the exponent for running time is $1+x^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}(e_{h}(k+1-a^{\prime})-1)=1+x_{a}(e_{h}(k-a)-1)$ and the bound on $S^{\prime}_{a^{\prime}}$ is $(\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{1-x_{a}}$ , both with same exponents as previous bounds.

We then compare exponents related to $S_{b}$ and $S^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}$ .

- • If $b>\ell$ . Then $b^{\prime}=b\geq\ell+1=\ell^{\prime}$ . Then $S_{b}$ in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ is bounded by $\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell}^{b/\ell})$ . In the $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm, $S_{b^{\prime}}^{\prime}$ is bounded by $\tilde{O}((\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{b/(\ell+1)})$ , a smaller exponent.

- • If $b=\ell$ . In this case, $S_{b}=\tilde{O}(\Delta_{\ell})$ and we will have $b^{\prime}<\ell^{\prime}$ . Let $x^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}=0$ in $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . Then $S^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}$ is bounded by $\tilde{O}((\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{1})$ , the same exponent as the bound of $S_{b}$ . Also, the cost for having this bound is $\tilde{O}((\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{1+x^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}(e_{h}(k+1-b^{\prime}))})=\tilde{O}(\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})$ , so we can ignore the cost as it is near-linear time.

- • If $b<\ell$ , the exponent of the running time for bounding $S_{b}$ in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ is $1+x_{b}(e_{h}(k-b)-1)$ , and $S_{b}$ is bounded by $\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}}$ . Let $x^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}$ be equal to $x_{b}$ in the algorithm for $(k+1,\ell+1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . Then notice that the exponent for running time is $1+x^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}(e_{h}(k+1-b^{\prime})-1)=1+x_{b}(e_{h}(k-b+1)-1)$ . By the induction assumption, $e_{h}(k-b+1)\leq e_{h}(k-b)$ , so $1+x_{b}(e_{h}(k-b+1)-1)$ is upper bounded by the running time exponent of the corresponding case in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . Note that this case does not happen in the base case $k=h+1$ , as $b<\ell=1$ can never happen, so we can safely apply the induction assumption. The bound on $S^{\prime}_{b^{\prime}}$ is $(\Delta^{\prime}_{\ell^{\prime}})^{1-x_{b}}$ , with the same exponent as $S_{b}$ in $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ .

The comparison of the exponents related to $S_{c}$ and $S^{\prime}_{c^{\prime}}$ works similarly. Thus, $e_{h}(k+1)\leq e_{h}(k)$ . ∎

#### Proposition 3.7.

$e_{h}(k)=1+O\left(1/k^{\log_{\frac{3}{2}}(\frac{\omega}{\omega-1})}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\ell=k-h$ . Let $k_{0}=100h$ . For all $k\leq k_{0}$ , $e_{h}(k)=O(1)$ .

For $k>k_{0}$ , we choose $a,b,c$ in our $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm so that $\lfloor k/3\rfloor=c\leq b\leq a=\lceil k/3\rceil$ . Clearly, $a,b,c<\ell=k-h$ . The running time of the algorithm is thus

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{a}\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{b}\cdot(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{c}\cdot(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}+MM\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{a}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{c}}\right)\right). $$

By Lemma 3.6, $e_{h}(k-c)\leq e_{h}(k-b)\leq e_{h}(k-a)$ , so the running time is bounded by

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1+\max\{x_{a},x_{b},x_{c}\}\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)}+MM\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{a}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{c}}\right)\right). $$

Set $x_{a}=x_{b}=x_{c}=\frac{\omega-1}{\omega+e_{h}(k-a)-1}$ . The running time then becomes

$$ \tilde{O}\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{\omega\cdot e_{h}(k-a)}{\omega+e_{h}(k-a)-1}}\right). $$

Thus, $e_{h}(k)\leq\frac{\omega\cdot e_{h}(k-a)}{\omega+e_{h}(k-a)-1}$ . Consequently,

$$ e_{h}(k)-1\leq\frac{(\omega-1)\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)}{\omega+e_{h}(k-a)-1}\leq\frac{\omega-1}{\omega}\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)=\frac{\omega-1}{\omega}\cdot(e_{h}(k-\lceil k/3\rceil)-1). $$

Therefore $e_{h}(k)-1\leq O\left(\left(\frac{\omega-1}{\omega}\right)^{\log_{\frac{3}{2}}k}\right)=O\left(1/k^{\log_{\frac{3}{2}}(\frac{\omega}{\omega-1})}\right)$ . ∎

We also show that our choices of $a,b,c$ are not too far away from optimal, at least when $\omega=2$ . In the following proposition, recall $e_{h}(k)$ is the exponent of our algorithm, instead of the best exponent for $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ .

#### Proposition 3.8.

$e_{h}(k)=1+\Omega\left(1/k^{\log_{\frac{3}{2}}(2)}\right)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\ell=k-h$ , $\rho=\log_{\frac{3}{2}}(2)$ , and $f_{h}(k)=\frac{1}{e_{h}(k)-1}$ . Let $k_{0}=100h$ . It is not difficult to see that for all $k\leq k_{0}$ , $f_{h}(k)\leq Mk^{\rho}-1$ for some sufficiently large constant $M>1$ because our algorithm does not achieve almost linear time, i.e., it always has $e_{h}(k)>1$ and thus $f_{h}(k)<\infty$ .

Let $k>k_{0}$ , and let $a,b,c$ be the optimal choices for $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ . We will show by induction that $f_{h}(k)\leq Mk^{\rho}-1$ . Consider two cases.

For the first case, assume $a<\ell$ . Let $x_{a},x_{b},x_{c}$ be the optimal parameters for $(k,k-h)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ , and if there are multiple choices, we choose one set of parameters with smallest $x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}$ . Then, the bound of our running time is (up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors)

$$ \Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{a}\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{b}\cdot(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{c}\cdot(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}+MM\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{a}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{c}}\right). $$

Suppose $x_{a}>x_{b}$ . By Lemma 3.6, $e_{h}(k-a)\geq e_{h}(k-b)$ . Therefore, we can slightly increase $x_{b}$ , and the running time of the algorithm will not be worse. This contradicts with the optimality of $x_{a},x_{b},x_{c}$ and minimality of $x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}$ . Thus, we must have $x_{a}\leq x_{b}$ . Similarly, we have $x_{b}\leq x_{c}$ .

Then we can lower bound $MM\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{a}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{c}}\right)$ by $\Delta_{\ell}^{2-x_{a}-x_{b}}$ .

The optimal way to balance $\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{a}\cdot(e_{h}(k-a)-1)},\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{b}\cdot(e_{h}(k-b)-1)},\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{c}\cdot(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}$ and $\Delta_{\ell}^{2-x_{a}-x_{b}}$ is to set $x_{a}=\frac{e_{h}(k-b)-1}{e_{h}(k-a)e_{h}(k-b)-1}$ , $x_{b}=\frac{e_{h}(k-a)-1}{e_{h}(k-a)e_{h}(k-b)-1}$ and $x_{c}=\min\{1,\frac{(e_{h}(k-a)-1)(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}{(e_{h}(k-a)e_{h}(k-b)-1)(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}\}$ , which gives

$$ e_{h}(k)\geq\frac{2e_{h}(k-a)e_{h}(k-b)-e_{h}(k-a)-e_{h}(k-b)}{e_{h}(k-a)e_{h}(k-b)-1}. $$

Substituting $e_{h}$ by $f_{h}$ gives the following cleaner formula:

$$ f_{h}(k)\leq 1+f_{h}(k-a)+f_{h}(k-b). $$

As the algorithm chooses the optimal $a,b,c$ , we have that

$$ f_{h}(k)\leq\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq c\leq b\leq a\leq k\\
a+b+c=k\end{subarray}}\left\{1+f_{h}(k-a)+f_{h}(k-b)\right\}. $$

By Lemma 3.6, $f_{h}(k-b)$ is nondecreasing when $b$ increases, so we can pick $b$ to be as large as possible for fixed $a$ . Therefore, for fixed $a$ , we choose $c=\lfloor\frac{k-a}{2}\rfloor$ and $b=\lceil\frac{k-a}{2}\rceil$ . Therefore, we can rewrite

$$ f_{h}(k)\leq\max_{k/3\leq a\leq k-2}\left\{1+f_{h}(k-a)+f_{h}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k+a}{2}\right\rfloor\right)\right\}. $$

By the induction assumption, $f_{h}(k^{\prime})\leq M(k^{\prime})^{\rho}-1$ for all $k^{\prime}<k$ .

Then,

$$ \displaystyle f_{h}(k) \displaystyle\leq\max_{k/3\leq a\leq k-2}\left\{1+f_{h}(k-a)+f_{h}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k+a}{2}\right\rfloor\right)\right\} \displaystyle\leq\max_{0\leq p\leq k/3}\left\{1+M\left(\frac{2k}{3}-2p\right)^{\rho}+M\left(\frac{2k}{3}+p\right)^{\rho}-2\right\} \displaystyle\leq Mk^{\rho}\cdot\max_{0\leq p^{\prime}\leq 1/3}\left\{\left(\frac{2}{3}-2p^{\prime}\right)^{\rho}+\left(\frac{2}{3}+p^{\prime}\right)^{\rho}\right\}-1 \displaystyle\leq Mk^{\rho}-1, $$

which completes the induction step for this case.

For the other case, assume $a\geq\ell$ . Note that we must have $b,c<\ell$ as $2\ell>k$ . Let $x_{b},x_{c}$ be the optimal parameters. Similar as before, we can assume $x_{b}\leq x_{c}$ . Then, the bound of our running time is (up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors)

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{b}\cdot(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{c}\cdot(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}+MM\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{a/\ell},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{b}},\Delta_{\ell}^{1-x_{c}}\right) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{b}\cdot(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{1+x_{c}\cdot(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}+\Delta_{\ell}^{a/\ell+1-x_{b}} $$

The optimal way to balance is to set $x_{b}=\frac{a}{\ell e_{h}(k-b)}$ and $x_{c}=\min\{1,\frac{a(e_{h}(k-b)-1)}{\ell e_{h}(k-b)(e_{h}(k-c)-1)}\}$ . This gives $e_{h}(k)\geq\frac{ae_{h}(k-b)-a}{\ell e_{h}(k-b)}+1$ . Note that it is possible that $x_{b}>1$ in this setting, but if that happens, $e_{h}(k)>e_{h}(k-b)$ , which by Lemma 3.6, can never be optimal. In terms of $f_{h}$ , this implies that $f_{h}(k)\leq\frac{\ell(f_{h}(k-b)+1)}{a}$ . As the algorithm chooses the optimal $a,b,c$ , we have that

$$ f_{h}(k)\leq\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq c\leq b<\ell\leq a\leq k\\
a+b+c=k\end{subarray}}\frac{\ell(f_{h}(k-b)+1)}{a}. $$

By Lemma 3.6, $f_{h}(k-b)$ is nondecreasing when $b$ increases, so we can pick $b$ to be as large as possible for fixed $a$ . Therefore, for fixed $a$ , we choose $c=\lfloor\frac{k-a}{2}\rfloor$ and $b=\lceil\frac{k-a}{2}\rceil$ . Thus, we can rewrite

$$ f_{h}(k)\leq\max_{\ell\leq a\leq k-2}\frac{\ell(f_{h}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k+a}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+1)}{a}\leq\max_{\ell\leq a\leq k-2}\left\{f_{h}\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k+a}{2}\right\rfloor\right)+1\right\}. $$

By induction, it can be further upper bounded by

$$ \max_{\ell\leq a\leq k-2}\left\{M\left(\left\lfloor\frac{k+a}{2}\right\rfloor\right)^{\rho}-1+1\right\}\leq M(k-1)^{\rho}<Mk^{\rho}-1, $$

as $M,\rho>1$ . This finishes the induction step for this case.

Overall, we have shown that $f_{h}(k)\leq Mk^{\rho}-1$ for all $k$ , which implies $e_{h}(k)=1+\Omega\left(1/k^{\log_{\frac{3}{2}}(2)}\right)$ . ∎

### 3.4 Upper Bound for $(C\ell,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$

Define a sequence of functions $(f_{i})_{i\geq 0}$ as follows:

$$ f_{i}(C)=\frac{2^{i}\omega^{i+1}C}{3^{i+1}(\omega-1)^{i}+\left(3(2^{i}-3^{i})(\omega-1)^{i}-2^{i}(\omega-1)^{i}\omega+2^{i}\omega^{i+1}\right)C}. $$

The functions have the following recurrence relation, whose proof we omit as it is straightforward algebra.

#### Claim 3.9.

$f_{0}(C)=\frac{\omega C}{3}$ and $f_{i}(C)=\frac{\omega}{1+\frac{\omega-1}{f_{i-1}\left(\frac{2C}{3-C}\right)}}$ for $i>0$ .

Then we can express the running time of $(C\ell,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ for sufficiently large $\ell$ in terms of the functions $f_{i}$ :

#### Theorem 3.10.

Let $C>1$ be any constant such that $\frac{1}{C}\in\left(1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{i},1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{i+1}\right]$ for some constant integer $i\geq 0$ . Then for any $\ell\geq 1$ and $C\ell\leq k\leq(C+o_{\ell}(1))\ell$ , $g(k,\ell)\leq f_{i}(C)+o_{\ell}(1)$ .

#### Proof.

We prove by induction on $i$ .

When $i=0$ , $k\geq C\ell\geq 3\ell$ . Therefore, we can apply the $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ example in Section 3.2 for $\ell\leq\lfloor k/3\rfloor$ to get $g(k,\ell)\leq\omega(\lceil k/3\rceil,\lceil(k-1)/3\rceil,\lfloor k/3\rfloor)/\ell$ . This leads to

$$ \displaystyle g(k,\ell) \displaystyle\leq\omega(k/3+1,k/3+1,k/3+1)/\ell \displaystyle=\frac{(k/3+1)\omega}{\ell} \displaystyle\leq\frac{((C+o_{\ell}(1))\ell/3+1)\omega}{\ell} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\omega C}{3}+o_{\ell}(1)=f_{0}(C)+o_{\ell}(1). $$

When $i>0$ , assume the claim is correct for $i-1$ . Similar to the proof of Proposition 3.7, we choose $a,b,c$ in our $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ algorithm so that $\lfloor k/3\rfloor=c\leq b\leq a=\lceil k/3\rceil$ . By the same analysis, the running time exponent can then be bounded by $\frac{\omega\cdot g(k-a,\ell-a)}{\omega+g(k-a,\ell-a)-1}$ . Let $C^{\prime}=\frac{2C}{3-C}$ . It is not difficult to verify that $\frac{1}{C^{\prime}}\in\left(1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{i-1},1-\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{i}\right]$ .

Also,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k-a}{\ell-a} \displaystyle\geq\frac{k-k/3}{\ell-k/3}\geq\frac{C\ell-(C\ell)/3}{\ell-(C\ell)/3}=\frac{2C}{3-C}=C^{\prime}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\frac{k-a}{\ell-a} \displaystyle\leq\frac{k-(k/3+1)}{\ell-(k/3+1)}\leq\frac{(C+o_{\ell}(1))\ell-((C+o_{\ell}(1))\ell)/3}{\ell-((C+o_{\ell}(1))\ell)/3}=\frac{2C+o_{\ell}(1)}{3-C-o_{\ell}(1)}=C^{\prime}+o_{\ell}(1). $$

Thus, $C^{\prime}(\ell-a)\leq k-a\leq(C^{\prime}+o_{\ell}(1))(\ell-a)$ , so $g(k-a,\ell-a)\leq f_{i-1}(C^{\prime})+o_{\ell}(1)$ by induction. Therefore, the running time exponent of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Detection}$ can be bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\omega\cdot g(k-a,\ell-a)}{\omega+g(k-a,\ell-a)-1} \displaystyle=\frac{\omega}{1+\frac{\omega-1}{g(k-a,\ell-a)}}\leq\frac{\omega}{1+\frac{\omega-1}{f_{i-1}(C^{\prime})+o_{\ell}(1)}}\leq\frac{\omega}{1+\frac{\omega-1}{f_{i-1}(\frac{2C}{3-C})}}+o_{\ell}(1)=f_{i}(C)+o_{\ell}(1). $$

∎

The actual exponents are computed by dynamic programming. ## 4 Lower Bounds for Listing Cliques

In this section, we will show our conditional lower bound for $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ under the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis.

#### Theorem 4.1 (Theorem 1.10).

For any $k\geq 3,1\leq\ell<k$ , and $\gamma\in[0,k/\ell]$ , $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for instances with $t=\tilde{\Theta}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma})$ requires

$$ \left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-o(1)} $$

time, where $\Delta_{\ell}$ is the number of $\ell$ -cliques and $t$ is the number of $k$ -cliques required to list, assuming Hypothesis 1.3.

#### Proof.

First, we can assume $\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}+\gamma(1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)})>1$ , as otherwise the lower bound is trivial.

Let $G=(V=V_{1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_{k},E,w)$ be a $k$ -partite Exact- $k$ -Clique instance on $k\cdot n$ nodes. Without loss of generality, we assume the edge weights $w$ of $G$ are from $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ for some sufficiently large prime $p=n^{O(k)}=n^{O(1)}$ . Then we sample $x\sim\mathbb{F}_{p}$ uniformly at random. For every $i\in[k]$ , and every node $v\in V_{i}$ , we sample $k-1$ random variables $(y_{v,j})_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}\sim\mathbb{F}_{p}$ where $\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{v,j}=0$ uniformly at random. Note that $(y_{v,j})_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}$ are $(k-2)$ -wise independent.

For every $1\leq i<j\leq k$ , and $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ , let

$$ w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})=x\cdot w(v_{i},v_{j})+y_{v_{i},j}+y_{v_{j},i}. $$

It is not difficult to verify that, whenever $x\neq 0$ , the sets of exact- $k$ -cliques in the graph with weight $w$ and with weight $w^{\prime}$ are the same.

Then we partition $\mathbb{F}_{p}$ into $s$ contiguous intervals, each of length $O(p/s)$ , for some $s$ to be chosen later where $\Omega(1)\leq s\leq O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ . Consider all combinations of intervals $(L_{i,j})_{1\leq i<j\leq k}$ , where $0\in\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}L_{i,j}$ . If we fix an arbitrary choice of the first $\binom{k}{2}-1$ intervals, their sumset is an interval of length $O(p/s)$ . Thus, there is only $O(1)$ choices for the last interval in order for their sumset to contain $0$ . Hence, there are only $O(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1})$ such combinations. For each such combination, we construct an instance of $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ as follows: create an unweighted graph $H$ such that an edge $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ for $i<j$ in $G$ is added to $H$ if and only if $w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\in L_{i,j}$ . The high level idea then is to list a certain number of $k$ -cliques in $H$ and verify whether any of them is an exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . Clearly, this algorithm never finds an exact- $k$ -clique if $G$ does not have one, so it suffices to show that when $G$ does have an exact- $k$ -clique, the algorithm finds it with decent probability.

Let $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ be an arbitrary exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . Clearly, there exists one combination of intervals such that all edges in this exact- $k$ -clique are in the corresponding subgraph $H_{0}$ . For any $i,j$ and edge $(v_{i},v_{j})\in V_{i}\times V_{j}$ , the edge is in $H_{0}$ only if $w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\in[-O(p/s),O(p/s)]$ , which happens with probability $O(1/s)$ as long as $\{u_{i},u_{j}\}\neq\{v_{i},v_{j}\}$ . The following lemma shows that the random variables $w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})$ are fairly independent.

#### Lemma 4.2.

If $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ is not an exact- $k$ -clique w.r.t. $w$ , and $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ shares exactly $c$ nodes indexed by $S$ with $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ , then the random variables

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<j\leq k\\
i\not\in S\text{ or }j\not\in S\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

#### Proof.

By symmetry, we can assume $|S|=[c]$ , and we need to show that

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}=\left\{x\cdot(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j}))+y_{u_{i},j}+y_{u_{j},i}-y_{v_{i},j}-y_{v_{j},i}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

Define $\alpha_{i,j}=w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})$ . Let $\beta$ be the sum of all the $\alpha_{i,j}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\beta \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\
1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}\alpha_{i,j}=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\alpha_{i,j} \displaystyle=x\cdot\left(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\right)+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{u_{i},j}-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}}y_{v_{i},j} \displaystyle=x\cdot\left(\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\right). $$

Since $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ is an exact- $k$ -clique whereas $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ is not, we have $\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(w(u_{i},u_{j})-w(v_{i},v_{j})\right)\neq 0$ . Therefore, $\beta$ is uniformly random.

Showing $\left\{\alpha_{i,j}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are independent is equivalent to showing that the variables are independent when one of the variables is replaced with the sums of the variables. Namely, it suffices to show $\left\{\alpha_{i,j}\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\\ (i,j)\neq(k-1,k)\end{subarray}}\cup\{\beta\}$ are independent.

Consider the following ordering of the variables:

$$ \beta,\alpha_{c+1,1},\ldots,\alpha_{c+1,c},\alpha_{c+2,1},\ldots,\alpha_{c+2,c+1},\ldots,\alpha_{k-1,1},\ldots,\alpha_{k-1,k-2},\alpha_{k,1},\ldots,\alpha_{k,k-2}. $$

Conditioned on the previous variables, all $\alpha_{j,i}$ variables in this list has an additive term $y_{u_{j},i}$ that is independent of all previous variables. Thus, this list of variables is independent. ∎

#### Corollary 4.3.

For any $\ell$ -clique on nodes $(v_{i})_{i\in T}$ in $G$ that shares exactly $c$ nodes indexed by $S$ with $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ , the random variables

$$ \left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in T\\
i<j\\
i\not\in S\text{ or }j\not\in S\end{subarray}} $$

are independent.

#### Proof.

By symmetry, we can assume $[T]=[\ell]$ and $[S]=[c]$ . We can complete this $\ell$ -clique to a nonzero $k$ -clique $(v_{1},\ldots,v_{k})$ (we can assume any $\ell$ -clique is in some nonzero $k$ -clique by adding hypothetical nodes to the graph in this analysis).

By Lemma 4.2, $\left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq k\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are independent, so $\left\{w^{\prime}(u_{i},u_{j})-w^{\prime}(v_{i},v_{j})\right\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}c+1\leq j\leq\ell\\ 1\leq i<j\end{subarray}}$ are also independent. ∎

Now we can compute the expected number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ . The number of $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ that share exactly $c$ nodes with $(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})$ is $O(n^{\ell-c})$ . By Corollary 4.3, each of them is in $H_{0}$ with probability $O\left(1/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}-\binom{c}{2}}\right)$ . Therefore, the expected number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is

$$ O\left(\sum_{c=0}^{\ell}n^{\ell-c}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}-\binom{c}{2}}\right)=O\left(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}\right), $$

since by our choice of $s=O(n^{2/(k-1)})$ , we have that $s^{\binom{c}{2}}=O(n^{c})$ .

Similarly, the expected number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is $O\left(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}\right)$ .

Therefore, by Markov’s inequality and union bound, with probability at least $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , the number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is at most $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ and the number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is at most $n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}$ .

Let $s=n^{\frac{k-\gamma\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\gamma\binom{\ell}{2}}}$ , so that $\frac{n^{k}}{s^{\binom{k}{2}}}=\left(\frac{n^{\ell}}{s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}}\right)^{\gamma}$ . We can verify that indeed $\Omega(1)\leq s\leq O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ . In fact, since $\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}+\gamma(1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)})>1$ , we can obtain a stronger upper bound $s=O\left(n^{\frac{k-\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}-1}-\delta}\right)$ for $\delta>0$ .

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that there is a $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ for instances with specified $t=\tilde{\Theta}(\Delta_{\ell}^{\gamma})$ with running time

$$ T(\Delta_{\ell},t)=O\left(\left(\Delta_{\ell}^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}t^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-{\varepsilon}}\right) $$

for some ${\varepsilon}>0$ . Then consider the following algorithm for Exact- $k$ -Clique:

- 1. First, hash the weights of the graph and enumerate $O(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1})$ graphs $H$ as described earlier.

- 2. Enumerate all $\ell$ -cliques in $G$ , and pre-compute which graphs $H$ contain each $\ell$ -clique. Since each $\ell$ -clique exists in $s^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}$ graphs $H$ , and this list of graphs can be listed efficiently, this step costs

$$ \tilde{O}\left(n^{\ell}\cdot s^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)\leq\tilde{O}\left(n^{\ell}\cdot\left(n^{\frac{k-\ell}{\binom{k}{2}-\binom{\ell}{2}-1}-\delta}\right)^{\binom{k}{2}-1-\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)\leq\tilde{O}(n^{k-\delta^{\prime}}) $$

for some $\delta^{\prime}>0$ .

- 3. From the previous step, we have a list of $\ell$ -cliques for each graph $H$ . If some $H$ contains more than $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ $\ell$ -cliques, we skip it. If it contains fewer than $0.99n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ $\ell$ -cliques, we add a complete $\ell$ -partite graphs with $n^{\prime}$ nodes on each part, for some $n^{\prime}$ , so that the total number of $\ell$ -cliques in the new graph reaches $0.99(n+n^{\prime})^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ . Clearly, $n^{\prime}=O(n)$ .

- 4. For graphs $H$ which we did not skip in the previous step, we run $\mathcal{A}$ on it with $t=n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}+1$ . For any $k$ -clique listed by $\mathcal{A}$ , we test whether it is an exact- $k$ -clique in $G$ . This step takes $s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\cdot T(\tilde{O}(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}),\tilde{O}(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}))$ time.

- 5. If any exact- $k$ -clique is found in the previous step, we return YES for the Exact- $k$ -Clique instance; otherwise, we return NO.

Clearly, if $G$ contains no exact- $k$ -clique, our algorithm is always correct. If $G$ contains any exact- $k$ -clique, let $H_{0}$ be the constructed graph containing it. As discussed previously, with probability $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , the number of $\ell$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ is at most $n^{\ell}\log n/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}$ and the number of $k$ -cliques in $H_{0}$ that do not correspond to exact- $k$ -cliques in $G$ is at most $n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}$ . In this case, we will not skip $H_{0}$ in Step 3, and listing $t=n^{k}\log n/s^{\binom{k}{2}}+1$ $k$ -cliques in Step 4 guarantees an exact- $k$ -clique. Thus, we will find an exact- $k$ -clique with probability $1-1/\Omega(\log n)$ , which can be boosted to $1-1/\mathop{\rm poly}(n)$ by repeating the algorithm $O(\log n)$ times.

Overall, this algorithm only needs time (besides the previous $\tilde{O}(n^{k-\delta^{\prime}})$ time)

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}\cdot\left(\left(n^{\ell}/s^{\binom{\ell}{2}}\right)^{\frac{2}{\ell(k-\ell)}}\left(n^{k}/s^{\binom{k}{2}}\right)^{1-\frac{2}{k(k-\ell)}}\right)^{1-{\varepsilon}}\right)=\tilde{O}\left(n^{k}\cdot\left(\frac{s^{\binom{k}{2}-1}}{n^{k}}\right)^{\varepsilon}\right). $$

As $s=O(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})$ , the above running time can be further upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(n^{k}\cdot\left(\frac{(n^{\frac{2}{k-1}})^{\binom{k}{2}-1}}{n^{k}}\right)^{\varepsilon}\right)=\tilde{O}\left(n^{k-\frac{2{\varepsilon}}{k-1}}\right), $$

contradicting the Exact- $k$ -Clique hypothesis. ∎

## 5 Optimal Listing Algorithms for Graphs with Many $k$ -Cliques

In this section, we give a $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm that is optimal for graphs with many $k$ -cliques under Hypothesis 1.3. This algorithm can be seen as a generalization of the densifying and sparsifying paradigm of [bjorklund2014listing].

We then show how we can extend this algorithm to obtain the conditionally optimal algorithms for all $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for graphs with many $k$ -cliques.

### 5.1 Algorithm

First, we describe the algorithm for $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ in Algorithm 5.1.

Algorithm 2 $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ Algorithm for large $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k}}$ , where $\gamma_{k}$ is defined in Theorem 5.4

```
Dense(G:=(V,E),n,t): • Input: Graph $G=(V,E)$ with $|V|\leq n$ and at most $t$ $k$ -cliques. • Output: List of $k$ -cliques in $G$ . • The Algorithm: 1. If $n<k$ , it returns no $k$ -cliques. 2. Choose a parameter $\lambda$ . Let an edge be $\lambda$ -light if it is in fewer than $\lambda$ $k$ -cliques. 3. Use the algorithm in Lemma 2.6 to obtain a list $L$ of all $(k-2)$ -cliques (there are at most $n^{k-2}$ such cliques). 4. Initialize an empty list $T$ . 5. Repeat the following $O(\lambda\log n)$ times: – Sample a subset $L^{\prime}$ of $L$ of size $|L|/\lambda$ . – Construct adjacency matrices $A$ and $\overline{A}$ where the rows are indexed by $V$ and columns are indexed by $L^{\prime}$ . – Let $A[v,C]=1$ if node $v$ is distinct from and adjacent to every node in the $(k-1)$ -clique $C$ , and set $A[v,C]=0$ otherwise. – Let $\overline{A}[v,C]=A[v,C]\cdot C$ , i.e. column $C$ contains entries 0 or $C$ . – Compute $B=A\cdot A^{T}$ and $\overline{B}=A\cdot\overline{A}^{T}$ . This takes $O(\mathsf{MM}(n,|L^{\prime}|,n))$ time. – For every edge $(u,v)\in E$ that is $\lambda$ -light, if $B[u,v]=1$ , add $(u,v,\overline{B}[u,v])$ to $T$ . 6. Output $T$ . 7. Delete all $\lambda$ -light edges from $E$ to obtain $E^{\prime}$ (all $\lambda$ -light edges are found in Step 5 w.h.p.). 8. Call Sparse $(G^{\prime}:=(V,E^{\prime}),\binom{k}{2}t/\lambda,t)$ .
Sparse(G:=(V,E),m,t): • Input: Graph $G=(V,E)$ with $|E|\leq m$ and at most $t$ $k$ -cliques. • Output: List of $k$ -cliques in $G$ . • The Algorithm: 1. If $m<\binom{k}{2}$ , it returns no $k$ -cliques. 2. Choose a parameter $x$ . 3. Find all nodes such that $\deg(v)\leq x$ , and call the $(k-1,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm in the neighbourhoods of all such nodes with $n^{\prime}=\deg(v)$ . 4. Delete all nodes in $V$ of degree less than $x$ to obtain set $V^{\prime}$ . 5. Call Dense $(G^{\prime}:=(V^{\prime},E\cap(V^{\prime}\times V^{\prime})),2m/x,t)$
```

#### Correctness.

It is clear that the ${\tt Sparse}$ algorithm finds all $k$ -cliques in the neighborhoods of low-degree nodes. At the end of the algorithm, since the graph has $\Delta_{\ell}$ $\ell$ -cliques and only nodes with degree at least $x$ , there are at most $2m/x$ nodes left in the graph.

Now, we argue that the ${\tt Dense}$ algorithm lists all $k$ -cliques containing $\lambda$ -light edges.

We argue that Step 5 finds all $\lambda$ -light edges with high probability. For every $(u,v)\in E$ , let $L_{u,v}$ denote the set of all $(k-2)$ -cliques that form $k$ -cliques with nodes $u$ and $v$ . Since we sample $L^{\prime}$ of size $|L|/\lambda$ , the probability that $L_{u,v}\cap L^{\prime}=K_{k-2}$ for any fixed $K_{k-2}\in L_{u,v}$ is

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)^{|L_{u,v}|-1}\geq\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\lambda}\right)^{\lambda-1}\geq\frac{1}{e\lambda}. $$

Therefore, by choosing $O(\lambda\log n)$ random sets of size $|L|/\lambda$ , with high probability, we find all $k$ -cliques containing $\lambda$ -light edges.

#### $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ when $\ell\geq 2$ .

To generalize this algorithm to $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ for $\ell\geq 2$ , we recursively use $(k-1,\ell-1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ to reduce the problem to $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}.$ At a high level, the algorithm considers all nodes $v$ in fewer than $x$ $\ell$ -cliques and recursively calls $(k-1,\ell-1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ to list all $k$ -cliques containing $v$ . See Algorithm 5.1. The correctness of Algorithm 5.1 can be shown as follows.

Algorithm 2 $(k,\ell)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ Algorithm for large $t\geq n^{\gamma_{k,\ell}}$ , where $\gamma_{k,\ell}$ is defined in Theorem 5.10

```
Input:AgraphGandalistLofallℓ-cliques.
Output:Allk-cliquesinthegraph.
The Algorithm: 1. Call a node $v$ light if $\Delta_{\ell}(v)\leq x$ , for some parameter $x$ . 2. For all light nodes, call $(k-1,\ell-1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ in the neighbourhoods to find all $k$ -cliques incident to $x$ . 3. Delete all light nodes and incident edges from $G$ . 4. Call the $(k,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ algorithm ${\tt Dense}(G^{\prime}:=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}),\ell\Delta_{\ell}/x,t)$ (from Algorithm 5.1).
```

#### Correctness.

It is clear that the algorithm lists all $k$ -cliques incident to low-degree nodes. Since all remaining nodes are in at least $x$ $\ell$ -cliques, and each $\ell$ -cliques contains at most $\ell$ nodes, we can bound the remaining number of nodes by $\ell\Delta_{\ell}/x$ .

To illustrate these algorithms, we first show simplified analyses of Algorithms 5.1 and 5.1 for the case of $k=4$ and $k=5$ assuming that $\omega=2$ in Section 5.2. We give more detailed analyses in terms of $\omega$ in Sections 5.3 and 5.4.

### 5.2 Analysis for $k=4$ and $k=5$ assuming $\omega=2$

In this section, we illustrate how to analyze the runtime for listing algorithm by considering the cases where $k=4$ or $k=5$ .

#### Proposition 5.1.

Suppose $\omega=2$ . Then, given a graph $G$ with $t$ 4-cliques,

- • $(4,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}(n^{3}+n^{2/3}t^{5/6})$ if $G$ has $n$ nodes.

- • $(4,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}(m^{3/2}+mt^{2/5}+m^{1/2}t^{3/4})$ if $G$ has $m$ edges.

- • $(4,3)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ can be solved in $\tilde{O}(\Delta^{6/5}+\Delta t^{1/5}+\Delta^{2/3}t^{1/2})$ if $G$ has $\Delta=\Delta_{3}$ triangles.

#### Proof.

Consider the ${\tt Dense}$ algorithm. In this case, $L$ is a list of all (up to $n^{2}$ ) edges. Therefore, the runtime of this step can be bounded by

$$ D^{\prime}(n,m,t)\leq n^{2}+\lambda\log n\cdot\mathsf{MM}(n,m/\lambda,n)+S(6t/\lambda,t)=\tilde{O}(n^{2}+\lambda n^{2}+nm)+S(6t/\lambda). $$

We can also upper bound $m$ by $n^{2}$ to obtain the following bound without a dependence on $n$ :

$$ D(n,t)\leq D(n,n^{2},t)\leq\tilde{O}(n^{3}+\lambda n^{2})+S(6t/\lambda,t). $$

assuming $\omega=2$ .

Consider the ${\tt Sparse}$ algorithm. In this case, we call $(3,1)$ -listing, which takes time $\tilde{O}(n^{2}+nt^{2/3})$ . Therefore (ignoring $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors),

$$ \displaystyle S(m,t) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\left(\deg(v)^{2}+\deg(v)\Delta_{4}(v)^{2/3}\right)+D^{\prime}(2m/x,m,t) \displaystyle\leq\sum_{v:\deg(v)\leq x}\left(\deg(v)\cdot x+\deg(v)^{1/3}\Delta_{4}(v)^{2/3}x^{2/3}\right)+D^{\prime}(2m/x,m,t) \displaystyle\leq mx+m^{1/3}t^{2/3}x^{2/3}+D^{\prime}(2m/x,m,t), $$

where we applied Hölder’s inequality as seen in Corollary 2.2.

#### $(4,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ analysis.

To obtain a runtime for $(4,1)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ , we unravel the recursion in $D(n,t)$ . Ignoring $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors in the following inequalities, we have

$$ \displaystyle D(n,t) \displaystyle\leq n^{3}+\lambda n^{2}+S(6t/\lambda,t) \displaystyle\leq n^{3}+\lambda n^{2}+\frac{tx}{\lambda}+\frac{tx^{2/3}}{\lambda^{1/3}}+D\left(\frac{12t}{\lambda x},t\right) $$

Choosing $\lambda=\max\{1,\frac{24t}{nx}\}$ , we have $\frac{12t}{\lambda x}\leq n/2$ , and the above runtime will be dominated by the first four terms up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors. Substituting this value of $\lambda$ , we obtain a runtime of

$$ D(n,t)\leq n^{3}+\frac{tn}{x}+nx^{2}+n^{1/3}t^{2/3}x. $$

Choosing

$$ x=\begin{cases}n&t\leq n^{5/2}\\
n^{8/3}/t^{2/3}&n^{5/2}\leq t\leq n^{14/5}\\
n^{1/3}t^{1/6}&t\geq n^{14/5}\end{cases}, $$

we obtain $D(n,t)=n^{3}+n^{2/3}t^{5/6}$ , as desired.

#### $(4,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ analysis.

To obtain a runtime for $(4,2)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ , we analyze the runtime of $S(m,t)$ . Here, we use our bound $D^{\prime}$ in terms of $n$ , $m$ and $t$ to get a tighter analysis (instead of just $n$ and $t$ ).

$$ \displaystyle S(m,t) \displaystyle\leq mx+m^{1/3}t^{2/3}x^{2/3}+D^{\prime}(2m/x,m,t) \displaystyle\leq mx+m^{1/3}t^{2/3}x^{2/3}+\frac{\lambda m^{2}}{x^{2}}+\frac{m^{2}}{x}+S(6t/\lambda,t). $$

Choosing $\lambda=\max\{1,\frac{12t}{m}\}$ , we have that $6t/\lambda\leq m/2$ . Therefore, the first four terms dominate up to $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors, so (ignoring $\tilde{O}(1)$ factors)

$$ \displaystyle S(m,t) \displaystyle\leq mx+m^{1/3}t^{2/3}x^{2/3}+\frac{mt}{x^{2}}+\frac{m^{2}}{x}. $$

By choosing

$$ x=\begin{cases}m^{1/2}&\text{if $t\leq m^{5/4}$}\\
m/t^{2/5}&\text{if $m^{5/4}<t\leq m^{10/7}$}\\
m^{1/4}t^{1/8}&\text{if $t>m^{10/7}$,}\end{cases} $$

we get a runtime of

$$ S(m,t)\leq m^{3/2}+mt^{2/5}+m^{1/2}t^{3/4}. $$

#### $(4,3)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ analysis.

Note that while we can use Algorithm 5.1 to bound the runtime in this case, we instead provide a more efficient algorithm shown in Algorithm 5.2 for $(4,3)\text{-}\mathsf{Clique}\text{-}\mathsf{Listing}$ .
